uncited: This family of methods addresses the fundamental limitation of vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS): the production of "floating" volumetric ellipsoids that lack an explicit, watertight geometric boundary [Surface and Geometry Alignment](9267-surface-and-geometry-alignment.md).

By aligning the discrete Gaussian representation with continuous geometric priors (such as SDFs, depth maps, or explicit meshes), these methods enforce positional and normal consistency to enable accurate mesh extraction, physically-based rendering, and robust initialization [Surface and Geometry Alignment](9267-surface-and-geometry-alignment.md).

Unlike sibling methods that may rely solely on photometric loss or implicit constraints, this family explicitly integrates geometric supervision into the training or post-processing pipeline to ensure the Gaussians conform to physical surfaces [Surface and Geometry Alignment](9267-surface-and-geometry-alignment.md).
All methods in this family share the goal of aligning the discrete Gaussian representation with a continuous geometric prior [Surface and Geometry Alignment](9267-surface-and-geometry-alignment.md).
The core mechanism involves adding geometric loss terms to the standard photometric rendering loss $\mathcal{L}_{rgb}$ [Surface and Geometry Alignment](9267-surface-and-geometry-alignment.md).

**Positional Consistency:** Gaussian centers $\mathbf{c}_i$ are encouraged to lie on the zero-level set of a distance function (SDF or UDF) or align with metric depth estimates [Surface and Geometry Alignment](9267-surface-and-geometry-alignment.md).

**Normal Consistency:** The orientation of the Gaussians (derived from their covariance matrix or rotation quaternion) is aligned with the surface normal estimated from the geometric prior [Surface and Geometry Alignment](9267-surface-and-geometry-alignment.md).
where $\mathcal{L}_{geo}$ is the geometric consistency loss and $\mathcal{L}_{norm}$ is the normal consistency loss [Surface and Geometry Alignment](9267-surface-and-geometry-alignment.md).

The weights $\lambda_{geo}$ and $\lambda_{norm}$ are hyperparameters that balance photometric fidelity against geometric accuracy [Surface and Geometry Alignment](9267-surface-and-geometry-alignment.md).

NeuSG [9172-neusg] integrates the NeuS implicit surface reconstruction method into the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation to transfer explicit surface properties to the discrete Gaussian primitives [9172-neusg].
It solves the problem of vanilla 3DGS producing "floating ellipsoids" rather than coherent surfaces by enforcing geometric consistency [9172-neusg].
Unlike siblings that use monocular depth or explicit mesh extraction, NeuSG directly couples a NeuS-style Signed Distance Function (SDF) with a Gaussian rasterizer [9172-neusg].

GSDF [9205-gsdf] is a training optimization technique that aligns the discrete 3D Gaussian representation with a continuous Signed Distance Function (SDF) prior to enhance geometry reconstruction quality [9205-gsdf, S1].

It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [NeuSG](9172-neusg.md) by explicitly transferring surface properties from a neural SDF to the Gaussians, encouraging Gaussian centers to lie on the zero-level set and normals to align with the SDF gradient [9205-gsdf, S1].
The problem of "floating" Gaussians in standard 3DGS has been a primary driver for geometric priors [Surface and Geometry Alignment](9267-surface-and-geometry-alignment.md).
Early works like NeuSG [9172-neusg] adapted implicit surface representations (NeuS) to guide Gaussian placement [9172-neusg].

More recent approaches leverage monocular depth estimators for scale alignment [9183-monocular-depth-scale-alignment, S1] or sparse-view reconstruction [9185-sparse-view-3d-gaussian-splatting-with-depth-priors, S1].
